clue.text: Statesman gives talk on food

parts.note: a cured meat, one kind of food

explanation.surface: A politician gives an after-dinner speech about what is on the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down-the-page reading 'on' would mean 'above', but here it just puts the talk before the food.
explanation.definitionFit: William Pitt the Elder, the eighteenth-century British prime minister, was made Earl of Chatham and is often called simply Chatham.

clue.text: Is Barbara on board?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the surname of Barbara, the British Labour cabinet minister of the 1960s and 70s
second meaning: a chess piece, also called a rook, that stands on the board

explanation.surface: Has Barbara come aboard yet?
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' sounds like boarding a ship; it is a chessboard. Barbara Castle was a well-known British Labour politician.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a famous politician's surname and a piece placed on a chessboard.

clue.text: On the other side, as T. E. Lawrence once was

parts.note: Lawrence of Arabia later enlisted in the RAF as an aircraftman, abbreviated A/C
the alias he enlisted under was John Hume Ross

explanation.surface: Lawrence of Arabia was once on the opposing side.
explanation.walkthrough: After Arabia, Lawrence hid in the ranks of the RAF as Aircraftman Ross.
explanation.definitionFit: Across means on or to the far side of something, as in across the road.

clue.text: Not necessarily Turpin's way

parts.note: surface reading: not the method Dick Turpin would use
setter's reading: the highwayman worked the high roads, and this is a way that is high but not his kind of road

explanation.walkthrough: Dick Turpin was an eighteenth-century English highwayman who robbed travellers on the highway; this road is 'high' too, but in a town.
explanation.definitionFit: A high street is a town's main shopping street, a road but not the open highway a robber worked.

clue.text: Girl gives mournful opening song

indicators.note: an opening is the start, so only the beginning of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A girl sings a sad song to start the show.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria is a common girl's name, so it can stand for a girl.

clue.text: The girl in pink, perhaps?

parts.note: surface reading: a girl dressed in pink
setter's reading: pink is a gentle shade of red, so the girl's name is a description of the colour

explanation.walkthrough: Pink is a mild red; split the girl's name as MILD RED and it describes the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Mildred is a woman's first name whose two halves happen to describe a pale red, which pink is.

clue.text: Hume's coat appears odd — but it might grow on one!

indicators.note: something that looks odd is out of its normal shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The philosopher Hume's coat looks strange, though it might grow on you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grow on one' sounds like an idiom for coming to like something; here it is literal, hair growing on a face.
explanation.definitionFit: A moustache is facial hair grown on the upper lip, so it literally grows on a person.

clue.text: Title of song about dunderhead

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the song is wrapped around the other piece

parts.note: a lay is a short poem or song

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter of the word is used

parts.note: the head of the word dunder, its first letter

explanation.surface: The name of a song about a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dunderhead' looks like the word for a fool, but it splits into dunder and head.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady is a British title of rank, used for the wife of a lord or knight.

clue.text: Wild letters to Mr Cain

indicators.note: the letters of the next words are to be used freely in a new order

explanation.surface: Passionate letters written to a man called Cain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' would usually be the anagram signal; here it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Romantic can mean fanciful, unrestrained and idealistic, as in a wild, romantic landscape or notion.

clue.text: Dour leader gets sport suspended

indicators.note: the leader goes first, so only the opening letter of the word counts

explanation.surface: A grim team captain has a game called off.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dangling hangs loosely from a point, that is, it is suspended.

clue.text: Meat is enough to choke one?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the bony neck end of mutton, a cheap cut
second meaning: to throttle someone, to wring their neck

explanation.surface: A lump of tough meat that could make someone choke if swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrag is both a cut of meat from the neck and a verb for seizing someone by the neck and throttling them.

clue.text: Perhaps he delivers ammunition to someone

definitions.text: Perhaps he delivers ammunition to someone

parts.words: Perhaps he delivers ammunition to someone
parts.note: surface reading: someone supplying bullets or shells
setter's reading: rounds are cartridges, and a tradesman who delivers on a regular route makes his rounds

explanation.walkthrough: Rounds are units of ammunition, and a man who delivers milk or bread on a regular route is named after his rounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A roundsman is a tradesman's delivery man who calls at houses along a fixed route each day.

clue.text: Declines socially, as Cole's set might do

indicators.note: 'set' as in set the words in a new order, and 'might do' says this rearrangement could be done

parts.note: the letters taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone slips down the social ladder, the way Cole's crowd might.
explanation.walkthrough: Cole's set sounds like a social circle; the words 'as Cole's set' are in fact the ten letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose caste is an idiom for dropping in social rank or standing, from the Indian caste system.

clue.text: Dye makes a bad mark?

parts.note: a score of nothing, the worst mark there is

explanation.surface: A dye that leaves an ugly stain.
explanation.definitionFit: Anil is the indigo plant and the blue dye made from it.

clue.text: Combatants are pleased one's holding the list up

indicators.note: holding something means having it inside, so one piece sits within another
in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Fighters are happy someone is propping up the roster.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladiators were men who fought in Roman arenas, combatants by trade.

clue.text: Rogue knocks before visit — is to take charge

parts.note: knocks sharply, as on a door
to pay a call is to visit
cryptic: an ion is an atom that has taken on an electric charge

explanation.surface: A rogue bangs on the door before paying a visit, meaning to take over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take charge' sounds like assuming command, but here it is electrical: an ion is a charged particle.
explanation.definitionFit: A rapscallion is a mischievous rascal or scoundrel, an old-fashioned word for a rogue.

clue.text: Trains juvenile to make cakes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a nursery word for railway trains
second meaning: small fried dough balls, a West African snack

explanation.surface: Coaching a youngster in baking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trains' looks like a verb, coaching someone; it is the plural noun, and 'juvenile' says the word is child's talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Children call steam engines puff-puffs after their noise, and puff-puffs are also little doughnut-like cakes.

clue.text: Attribute breakdown to cider indeed!

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside another, here inside the word that follows
a breakdown splits something apart, so these letters are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: read as in deed: a deed is an act, and the cider letters go in it

explanation.surface: Blaming someone's collapse on drinking cider, of all things!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indeed' looks like an exclamation of emphasis; split it as in deed, so the scrambled cider goes inside a word for deed.
explanation.definitionFit: To accredit something to a person is to credit or ascribe it to them, which is attributing it.

clue.text: Informs of one's appearance in the papers, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says the word might take another form, so its letters are reordered
to make an appearance in something is to be found within it

explanation.surface: Tells someone about their photo in the newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: To apprise someone is to tell them of something, a formal synonym for informs.

clue.text: Dickensian takes money, if led astray

indicators.note: led astray means led off the proper path, so these letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: A Dickens character accepts a bribe and is corrupted.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'led astray' describes the man; in the wordplay it scrambles 'if led'.
explanation.definitionFit: David Copperfield is the title character of Dickens's novel, so he is a Dickensian figure.

clue.text: Leader gets in minced veal for the recess

indicators.note: minced meat is chopped up, so these letters are cut up and remixed
getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside the other

explanation.surface: The boss tucks into minced veal during the break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recess' looks like a lunch break; it is a nook in a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a small recess set back into the wall of a room.

clue.text: Flowers are like the rest? Wrong

indicators.note: something wrong is out of its correct order, so these letters are placed differently

parts.note: as means like, in the same way

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether these flowers match the others and is told they do not.
explanation.definitionFit: Asters are daisy-like garden flowers, often called Michaelmas daisies.

clue.text: Uncommon members of the bar, aren't they?

indicators.note: members belong to a larger body, so the letters are part of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A wry remark that barristers are an unusual breed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members of the bar' looks like lawyers, but it signals letters held within the words 'bar, aren't'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare and uncommon are synonyms: both describe something seldom found or seen.

clue.text: Celts' capes set off the pageants

indicators.note: to set something off is to start it moving, so these letters are sent into a new order

explanation.surface: Cloaks worn by Celtic performers show off the costumed parades.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectacle is a grand public show or display, which is what a pageant is.

clue.text: Fish perhaps dismissed someone?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: what an angler lands
second meaning: in cricket a ... is a ball held by a fielder, which puts the batsman out

explanation.surface: Was the fish perhaps sacking somebody?
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket batsmen are out, or dismissed, when a fielder holds the ball before it bounces.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch is a haul of fish, and also a fielding dismissal in cricket.

clue.text: A trunk to take over, say?

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: in cricket a bowler bowls each over of six balls

explanation.surface: Taking charge of a trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take over' sounds like assuming control; in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries, and to take one is to bowl it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bole is the main trunk of a tree.

clue.text: Balk of record, if Tom is out of form

indicators.note: something out of form has lost its proper shape, so these letters lose their order

explanation.surface: Tom's poor form leads to a hesitation on the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of form' reads like a sportsman's slump; it scrambles 'if Tom'. Balk here is the verb meaning thwart.
explanation.definitionFit: To discomfit originally meant to defeat or frustrate someone's plans, which is what balking them does.

clue.text: Main source of health, some say

definitions.text: Main source of health, some say

parts.words: Main source of health, some say
parts.note: surface reading: the chief cause of good health
setter's reading: the main is the sea, and the bracing seaside air was popularly thought to be healthy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is an old word for the sea. Victorians believed the fresh smell at the seaside was a health-giving gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaside air was popularly called ozone and claimed to be good for you, though the belief was folklore.

clue.text: Are they trying to find old coins?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people who try things out
second meaning: the tester was a Tudor silver coin, an early shilling

explanation.surface: Are these people searching for antique money?
explanation.definitionFit: Testers are those who try or trial something, and also an obsolete coin of Henry VIII's reign.

clue.text: She's entertaining a Nazi going round Ringway

indicators.note: going round something means encircling it, so one part wraps the rest

parts.note: split as ring (O, round like the letter) and way (ST, the abbreviation for street)

explanation.surface: A woman is entertaining a Nazi travelling through Ringway, Manchester's airport.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringway reads as one place name but splits into ring and way. Ringway was the old name of Manchester Airport, which fits an air hostess.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostess is a woman who receives and entertains guests, so the definition describes her role.
